$comment: Registry of BUILT widgets, consumed by the gallery page and scripts/build.mjs. `title` is the gallery card AND the page heading: they used to be allowed to differ, the card naming the topic and the page asking the question, and that split was cut — a student who clicked "Hypothesis Testing" should land on a page that says so. `npm run check` asserts manifest.title === defineWidget({title}) === the index.html <title> prefix; the question belongs in `subtitle`. `blurb` is gallery copy and nothing else reads it. The plan — every candidate concept, its target misconception and evidence — lives in docs/catalogue.md; see that file for why the two are separate. A widget marked shipped there must appear here, and vice versa. NO HEIGHT IS RECORDED HERE, and adding one back needs a reader for it first. It used to live in three files and drift; deleting the embedders (prd §6) left one copy that nothing consumed, and a number nothing reads is a number that drifts silently — by the time it was measured, eight of the nine were 190–310px wrong. Heights are also no longer one number per widget: `bayesian` returns a different one per tab. README's iframe recipe says how to get a correct one.

widgets.title: The Normal Distribution
widgets.blurb: Many small random nudges, added together, land in a bell curve.

widgets.title: Central Limit Theorem
widgets.blurb: The mean of a sample goes normal whatever the population looks like.

widgets.title: Bootstrap Sampling
widgets.blurb: Resample your one sample to see how uncertain its mean really is.

widgets.title: Confidence Intervals
widgets.blurb: Build the same studies' intervals three ways — bootstrap, normal, t — and watch how often each actually contains the true mean. At n = 5 the normal one misses far more than 1 time in 20.

widgets.title: Hypothesis Testing
widgets.blurb: Shuffle the group labels to see what chance alone could have produced.

widgets.title: Multiple Testing
widgets.blurb: Test twenty thousand genes at p < 0.05 and about a thousand come back significant even when none of them is different. Then see what correcting for it costs.

widgets.title: Power and Error Rates
widgets.blurb: You choose the false positive rate; you do not choose the other one. Change the sample size and watch which of the two moves — and which does not budge.

widgets.title: Maximum Likelihood
widgets.blurb: Twelve gene counts, drawn once. Try a candidate mean and every count gets a height under it; multiply them and you have how probable that candidate makes exactly what you saw. Then estimate the dispersion the Poisson ignored, and watch a search over both stop moving after two steps.

widgets.title: Bayesian Estimation
widgets.blurb: The likelihood said which parameters make your counts most probable; it could not say how probable a parameter is. Multiply it by what you believed beforehand, divide by the total, and the curve you get has an area of 1. Twelve counts overwhelm your prior on the mean and barely touch your prior on the spread — and a fourth tab shows why a sampler never has to compute that total at all.

widgets.title: Expectation–Maximization
widgets.blurb: Set two populations, draw a sample from them, and the labels come off as it lands. Two curves are guessed at random; every person then reports what fraction of them belongs to each, and those fractions refit the curves. Repeat. The two populations come back almost exactly right — and a seventh of the individuals still end up in the wrong group, which is what a hard cluster label hides.

widgets.title: Probability Distributions
widgets.blurb: Eight distributions on one decision tree, and which one you need is settled by what you are measuring rather than by the shape of the data. Walk the tree — counting or measuring, is there a ceiling, does the chance move — and land on a distribution you can then watch being generated one draw at a time. Then read it: d, p, q and r as the four questions they each answer.

widgets.title: Odds Ratio and Relative Risk
widgets.blurb: One table, two ratios. They share a numerator and divide by different things, so the odds ratio always overstates — by 1% when the outcome is rare and 200% when it is not, with the effect never changing. Then run the same patients as a case-control study, enrolling every case and a few controls each, and watch the risk ratio go wherever your enrolment budget puts it while the odds ratio still estimates the population's.
